clinicalPearls: Impaired ability of the eustachian tube to ventilate and equalise pressure in the middle ear, producing aural fullness, muffled hearing, popping and sometimes discomfort
Obstructive dysfunction, in which the tube fails to open adequately, is the common form and is often associated with rhinitis, sinusitis, reflux or allergy
Symptoms characteristically worsen with pressure change, such as air travel or diving, and may fluctuate with upper respiratory infection
Otoscopy may show a retracted tympanic membrane, and tympanometry can demonstrate negative middle-ear pressure or a middle-ear effusion
Persistent dysfunction can lead to middle-ear effusion, tympanic membrane retraction, and over time retraction pockets or cholesteatoma
The patulous form, where the tube stays abnormally open, causes autophony and hearing one's own breathing, and is managed differently from the obstructive type
Initial management targets the underlying nasal and nasopharyngeal factors, with autoinflation and medical therapy; ventilation tubes or balloon dilation are options in selected refractory cases
Persistent unilateral effusion in an adult mandates examination of the nasopharynx to exclude a tumour
reference.pathophysiology: The eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx and normally opens intermittently, chiefly through tensor veli palatini action during swallowing, to ventilate the middle ear and equalise pressure. In obstructive dysfunction, inflammation, mucosal oedema, allergy, reflux, adenoidal hypertrophy or a nasopharyngeal mass impairs tubal opening, so the middle ear cannot be ventilated. Trapped air is absorbed by the mucosa, generating negative pressure that draws the tympanic membrane inward and can promote transudation of an effusion. Chronic negative pressure and retraction may lead to retraction pockets and cholesteatoma. In the less common patulous form the tube remains abnormally patent, transmitting nasopharyngeal sounds and causing autophony.
additionalDifferentials: Acute or chronic otitis media with effusion
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma or mass causing unilateral obstruction
Superior semicircular canal dehiscence and other third-window disorders causing autophony
additionalInvestigations: Otoscopy or microscopy to assess the tympanic membrane and detect effusion or retraction
Tympanometry to document middle-ear pressure and effusion
Pure-tone audiometry to characterise any conductive hearing loss
Nasal endoscopy and nasopharyngeal examination, essential in persistent unilateral disease
Cross-sectional imaging of the nasopharynx and skull base when a mass is suspected
redFlags: Persistent unilateral middle-ear effusion in an adult, which requires exclusion of nasopharyngeal carcinoma
Cranial nerve deficits, neck mass or epistaxis suggesting a nasopharyngeal tumour
Progressive retraction pocket or features suggesting developing cholesteatoma
Sudden hearing loss or vertigo indicating alternative inner-ear pathology
reference.prognosis: Many cases are self-limiting or improve once contributing nasal and nasopharyngeal factors are treated. A subset develops chronic effusion or tympanic membrane retraction that may require ventilation tubes or balloon dilation, and untreated chronic retraction can progress to cholesteatoma.
pitfalls: Failing to examine the nasopharynx in an adult with persistent unilateral effusion and missing a carcinoma
Confusing the patulous form with obstructive dysfunction and prescribing inappropriate decongestion
Overlooking progressive tympanic membrane retraction that heralds cholesteatoma
Attributing autophony to obstructive dysfunction without considering a third-window disorder
references: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Treat contributing nasal and nasopharyngeal factors with intranasal corticosteroids, antihistamines for allergic rhinitis, and management of reflux and sinusitis
Autoinflation and pressure-equalisation manoeuvres to open the tube and ventilate the middle ear
For persistent obstructive disease, balloon eustachian tuboplasty or insertion of ventilation (grommet) tubes
Monitor for and manage middle-ear effusion, tympanic retraction, retraction pockets and cholesteatoma
Nasal endoscopy and cross-sectional imaging to exclude a nasopharyngeal mass in persistent unilateral disease
For the patulous form, use nasal saline and weight restoration and avoid decongestants, as management differs from the obstructive type
